functional.text: For every API request, decide allow or deny against the caller's limits; denied requests are rejected with HTTP 429 and a retry hint.
Limits are rules keyed by user, API key or IP plus endpoint (e.g. 100/min per user, 5,000/hour per API key, strict login limit); operators change them at runtime without a deploy.
Callers can see their remaining quota and reset time in response headers.

non_functional.text: Low overhead: the decision adds < 5 ms at p99 latency to each request.
Limits hold across the fleet of ~40 API servers, not per server; a few % over-admission is acceptable.
The limiter must never take the API down with it; sensitive endpoints (login) are the exception.

assumptions.text: 10M active clients/day, peak 300k requests/s, ~2 rules match a request and ~3 rules can apply to a client.
~100 bytes per counter including key and store overhead.

out_of_scope.text: Billing for quota, and L3/L4 DDoS protection (handled by the network provider).

api.notes: Internal; in practice a library call inside the gateway rather than a network hop.

api.response: 200 with X-RateLimit-Limit/-Remaining/-Reset, or 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After

api.notes: Operators change limits without a deploy.

data.name: buckets
data.fields: key = bucket:{rule_id}:{client} → tokens, last_refill_ms; TTL = window
data.why: Hot, tiny, short-lived counter state; losing it only resets a few counts.

data.name: rules
data.fields: id, match (key_type, endpoint pattern), limit, window_s, burst, failure_mode (open|closed), version
data.why: Small, rarely written, needs auditing and versioned rollback; gateways cache it.

parts.title: Counting algorithm
parts.problem: Pick how a client's usage is counted so that '100 per minute' holds without boundary bursts, in a few bytes per key and one cheap update per request.

options.name: fixed window counter
options.pros: one integer per key; trivial INCR + EXPIRE
options.cons: a client can send 2× the limit across a window boundary (59 s + 0 s)

options.name: sliding log
options.cons: one timestamp per request: 5,000/hour per API key means up to 5,000 entries per key

options.name: sliding window counter
options.pros: two integers, smooths the boundary spike
options.cons: approximate (assumes even spread in the previous window)

options.name: token bucket
options.pros: two numbers per key; rate and burst are explicit; refill computed lazily
options.cons: needs a refill computation per call; burst size must be chosen

parts.choice: token bucket (tokens, last_refill_ms per rule + client)
parts.why: Fits the ~3 GB state budget (two numbers per key), lets product say 'limit + burst' directly, and refills lazily from last_refill_ms, so there are no timers. Fixed windows would let a client double the quota at every boundary.

parts.title: Shared counter store
parts.problem: Keep every client's counting state where all ~40 servers (or gateways) see the same value, at ~600k operations/s, within a 1–2 ms round trip.

options.name: in-memory counters on each server
options.cons: a user spread over 40 servers gets up to 40× the quota; restarts wipe counts

options.name: sticky routing by client to one server
options.cons: uneven load, rebalancing resets counts, couples the LB to limiting

options.name: SQL table of counters
options.cons: 600k writes/s of hot rows: far too slow and contended

options.name: sharded in-memory store (Redis Cluster) keyed by rule + client
options.pros: ~1 ms, ~100k ops/s per node, TTLs expire idle keys, scales by adding shards
options.cons: another tier to run; counts can reset on failover

parts.choice: sharded Redis Cluster holding the token buckets, keyed bucket:{rule}:{client}, with replicas
parts.why: State is tiny (≈ 3 GB) but hot: 600k ops/s ÷ 100k per node ≈ 6 primaries, 12 nodes with replicas. Losing a few counts on failover is acceptable under N2's 'roughly right'.

parts.title: Where the check runs
parts.problem: Choose the enforcement point so every request is judged exactly once, before it costs anything, without every team re-implementing the limiter.

options.name: library/middleware in each API service
options.cons: every service and language re-implements it; unprotected services slip through

options.name: sidecar proxy next to each service
options.cons: one sidecar per pod to roll out; checks happen after traffic already crossed the network

options.name: separate limiter service called per request
options.cons: an extra network hop on every request

options.name: API gateway (edge proxy) behind the load balancer
options.pros: one choke point every request already passes; rejects before the API servers do work
options.cons: the gateway tier must scale and stay up

parts.choice: API gateway behind the load balancer runs the limiter as an in-process filter before routing
parts.why: All public traffic already crosses the gateway, so the check costs one Redis round trip and no extra hop (N1). Rejected requests never reach the 40 API servers, and the 429 + X-RateLimit headers are added in one place (F3).

parts.title: Rules config and degraded mode
parts.problem: Let operators change limits without a deploy, get them to every gateway within seconds, and say per rule what happens when the counter store is unreachable.

options.name: limits hard-coded in gateway config
options.cons: every change is a deploy (breaks F2)

options.name: gateway reads the rules DB on every request
options.cons: a DB query per request: latency and a new single point of failure

options.name: rules DB behind a rules service, cached in each gateway and refreshed every few seconds
options.pros: fresh within seconds, zero cost per request, gateways keep the last good copy if the service is down
options.cons: a few seconds of staleness; needs versioning for rollback

parts.choice: rules DB + rules service; gateways cache the rule set and refresh it every 5 s; each rule carries failure_mode (open|closed)
parts.why: F2 without touching N1: rule lookups are local memory. Storing failure_mode on the rule lets product keep the API up (fail open) while security keeps login strict (fail closed), satisfying N3.

deep_dives.title: Concurrent updates to one bucket

options.name: read then write from the gateway
options.cons: race: two gateways both see 1 token and both allow

options.name: distributed lock per key
options.cons: an extra round trip and lock contention on hot keys

options.name: server-side atomic script (Lua)
options.pros: one round trip, serialised by the shard
options.cons: script must stay tiny; keys of one script must share a shard

deep_dives.choice: server-side atomic script (Lua) doing refill + take
deep_dives.why: The shard that owns the key runs the script atomically, so N2 holds without locks and N1 costs one ~1 ms round trip.

deep_dives.title: When the counter store is slow or down

options.name: fail closed
options.cons: the whole API goes down with the limiter

options.name: fail open
options.cons: no protection while the store is down

options.name: fail open with a local fallback limit
options.pros: API stays up with coarse per-gateway protection
options.cons: limits are approximate during the incident

deep_dives.choice: fail open with a local fallback limit; fail closed for rules marked sensitive (login)
deep_dives.why: N3: product prefers over-admission to an outage, security needs login protected. A 2 ms timeout triggers the fallback: an in-process bucket sized limit / number of gateways.

deep_dives.title: One abusive client on one shard (hot key)

options.name: do nothing
options.cons: one scraper at 50k req/s saturates the shard that owns its key

options.name: local pre-check in each gateway
options.pros: obviously-over clients are rejected without a Redis call
options.cons: slightly more over-admission at the edge of the limit

options.name: lease token batches to gateways
options.pros: one Redis call per N requests
options.cons: unused tokens are stranded in a gateway until the lease expires

deep_dives.choice: local pre-check: once a client is denied, the gateway caches the deny until reset_at
deep_dives.why: A denied client keeps retrying; caching the verdict locally until the reset time removes almost all of its Redis traffic at no accuracy cost.

wrapup.bottlenecks: A single hot client key concentrates on one shard (cache denies locally until reset_at); the gateway tier itself (scale horizontally behind the LB); the Lua script must stay O(1).
wrapup.failures: Shard loss: a replica is promoted and a few counts reset (acceptable). Store timeouts: fail open with a local fallback limit, fail closed for login. Bad rule push: rules are versioned and gateways can roll back. Rules service down: gateways keep the last good rule set.
wrapup.monitoring: Decision latency p99, store errors and timeouts, number of fail-open decisions, 429 rate per rule and per top client, hot-key detection, rules version per gateway.
wrapup.scale: 10× traffic: more gateway instances and more Redis shards (keys hash-partitioned); lease small token batches to gateways to cut store round trips.
wrapup.future: Per-region limits with async reconciliation, cost-based limits (expensive endpoints cost more tokens), self-serve quota dashboards.
